prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye. After the full exchange, no member disputes originality, maturity or independent reproduction, and nobody calls B018 premature. The achievement is one idea, Katori's magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the light shift while holding many atoms free of Doppler and recoil broadening, followed by Ye's group taking the clock to 1e-18 accuracy and many-body-limited operation. The result is measured, compared between laboratories on several continents, and already yields quantitative science: constancy of constants, ultralight dark-matter searches and gravitational redshift over millimetre scales. The two-name credit reflects the concept-plus-record structure without an arbitrary cut. I also note that Eriksson moved to B018 from a different opening first choice on scientific grounds, which is some evidence that the case survives scrutiny and is not only shared instrument-oriented taste. I want the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice clock specifically so that it does not read as a prize for optical clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The chair's challenge deserves a direct answer. Pearce's best argument is that IceCube opens a channel that did not exist, whereas lattice clocks extend a measurement we already knew how to make; on discovery character alone I accept that B007 has the stronger claim. The redefinition of the second is still pending, the comb (2005), laser cooling (1997) and ion control (2012) are all honoured foundations, and Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and ion-clock groups lie outside a two-name credit. I have not verified the priority sequence between early lattice proposals and first operating clocks and the committee has no member who has. These are real limitations, but each one affects the breadth of the citation, not the existence or reproducibility of the result.

responses.point: Pearce keeps IceCube (B007) first because it opens a new observational channel, and the chair's questions ask whether a new window should outrank a measured precision advance and whether any two- or three-name credit can be defended against the collaboration and its precursors.
responses.response: I have reconsidered and I still place B007 second, not first. On discovery character I concede Pearce's point that a new messenger is a different kind of achievement. What decides it for me is the credit question the chair himself poses. I cannot defend Halzen and Karle against a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA and Baikal precursors and the omission of Yoshida, and adding Yoshida within the three-person limit still leaves leadership and detector-construction roles that the supplied credit does not resolve. A prize whose citation we cannot assign to named people without arbitrary cuts is a weaker prize than one whose attribution is unusually clean, even if the underlying science is as significant. If the committee wanted B007 I would accept a diffuse-flux citation naming Halzen, Karle and Yoshida, but I would not rank it above B018.

responses.point: Johansson keeps Cirac and Zoller (B032) first as the theory that defined experimental fields, argues the 2012 prize does not cover the proposals, and now concedes that B018 has broader support and that his seventh place may reflect his field's habits.
responses.response: I appreciate that Johansson separates B032 from the 2012 prize, and I accept that a theory-only prize could be coherent. But the chair's overlap question is still unanswered: Cirac and Zoller also sit in B015 with Bloch and Greiner, so a B032 prize either pre-empts the cold-atom simulator case or forces a pairing that breaks the three-person limit. Where I do agree is that B032 is the strongest pure-theory case and certainly mature. My difference is that the experimental realisation of those proposals in ions and atoms was not itself the subject of a prize, so the citation would sound abstract. If Johansson can argue that the proposals can be cited precisely without touching B015, that is what would move me; his own concession on breadth of support makes me think he would accept B018 as a close second.

responses.point: Kroll supports B018 but asks whether the lattice step is separable from laser cooling (1997), the comb (2005) and ion control (2012), and whether the clean credit is bought by omitting competing clock lineages.
responses.response: I think the lattice step stands apart because it solved a specific problem that those earlier achievements did not: trapping many neutral atoms with the clock-transition light shift cancelled, which ions cannot do at comparable atom number. The ion-clock lineage reaches comparable accuracy by a different route, so a citation limited to the magic-wavelength lattice clock does not contradict it. The omission question is serious, though, and I agree that clean credit is not proof of completeness. For that reason I would keep the wording narrow and I would not claim in the citation that Katori and Ye invented optical clocks. That wording protects Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion groups from an implied exclusion without enlarging the list past what the three-person limit allows.

responses.point: Olsson, with Lindroth, wants the B018 citation kept narrow to lattice clocks, and notes that all six members who ranked B018 proposed the same two names.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow citation, and the uniform two-name proposal across six rankers is meaningful because it came from members with different fields and preferences. I would add a caution about the weight we put on it: agreement among members who rank it highly does not verify priority, and we have an acknowledged gap on the early lattice proposals. On timing I side with her view that the pending redefinition of the second does not need to delay the prize; the lattice-clock performance is established whatever the metrological bodies decide, and the redefinition is a consequence of the discovery, not its basis.

responses.point: Mehlig stands alone on fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B002), argues the experimental tests in tweezers and single molecules give it discovery character, and lists B018 as an alternative.
responses.response: I have weighed his defence of B002 and the chair's question about which result is the cited discovery. I still cannot answer it cleanly: the steady-state relation, Jarzynski's equality and trajectory-level entropy production are three separable steps, with Crooks the awkward omission and with contested priority for the steady-state relation. The experimental confirmations are real, but they confirm identities, so the prize would reward a framework more than a measured phenomenon. I therefore do not move to B002. I am glad that Mehlig lists B018 as an alternative, since it means the strongest candidate on credit clarity has support from outside the instrument-oriented members.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait; I think not, but this is a judgment about timing and not a fact I can check.
The priority sequence of early lattice proposals and first operating clocks is unverified by me and by every colleague, and an error there could change the credit.
How to weigh discovery character against attribution clarity; B007 would outrank B018 for me if a defensible three-name credit with clear roles existed.
Whether the unanimity on the two names reflects shared tastes in the room, which I discount, or an independent reading of the record.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none tied to B018, B007 or B032, and my own research in string theory and cosmology does not overlap with these candidates. As Secretary I have a procedural role, not a scientific stake in any candidate.
